Visual Analytics for Motor Vehicle Insurance

ISSS608 Visual Analytics Individual Assignment

Ang Ming Kwan

2026-05-15

Slide 1 | Executive Summary

A visual analytics investigation of 354,140 motor insurance policies from a Spanish non-life insurer (2022–2024) identifies structural profitability risks across product, demographic, behavioural, and geographic dimensions.

Four critical findings demand underwriting attention:

🔴 COMP_N (Comprehensive, No Excess): most loss-making product; 3.5% Bad-bonus policyholders confirms adverse selection; immediate actuarial review required

🔴 Bonus score: statistically validated predictor; loss ratio increases monotonically Good→Bad (all Wilcoxon p < 0.05); Bad-score policyholders drive disproportionate large-loss tail exposure

🟠 Short-duration policies: systematically higher loss ratios confirm claim-then-cancel behaviour; structural premium inadequacy

🟠 Glass claims are gateway events: bimodal frequency at 1–2 events/year confirms co-occurrence with broader claims; validates glass history as a renewal risk flag

Also: NB carries 2× adverse risk vs portfolio renewals · Bad-score policyholders: 75% retention · Urban > Rural loss ratios · Island pricing statistically unreliable

Slide 2 | Data Preparation

Import: Explicit semicolon delimiter via read_delim(): prevents silent mis-parsing of the 47-column, 354,140-row file.

Quality checks: Zero duplicates. Four variables with missing values: handled per-analysis (not global imputation), keeping each decision transparent.

Categorical recoding: Raw codes (e.g. "G", "NB", "U") replaced with labels. bonus_score converted to ordered factor: enabling correct ordering in Wilcoxon tests and ridgeline plots.

Outlier capping: 99th percentile cap on loss ratio and severity for visualisation only: all statistical tests use uncapped values.

Binning: Driver/vehicle age binned into actuarial bands. Vehicle brands classified into three tiers. claim_breadth (number of distinct claim lines per policy) derived as a behavioural signal variable.

Principle: Every wrangling decision is documented at the point of use: not globally applied,so the audit trail is always traceable.

fuel_type (0.36%) and vehicle_value (0.14%) are the only meaningful gaps. Impact on downstream analyses is minimal; excluded only in analyses that use those variables.

Slide 3 | Derived KPIs

Why raw data is insufficient: The dataset has premiums, claims, incurred costs, and exposure; but none of the actuarial metrics needed to assess profitability or volatility. Six KPIs were derived as the analytical backbone.

Exposure-adjustment is non-negotiable: A 3-month policy and a 12-month policy generate the same raw claim count for zero incidents. total_exposure (policy years) normalises all KPIs; without it, short-duration segments appear artificially safer.

Demographic variables tested: years_licensed and licence_age were derived to test whether driving experience predicts risk better than age.

⚠️ Data quality finding: Both variables showed near-zero Spearman ρ with claim frequency; because age_driving_licence records the calendar year of licence issue, not years of experience. years_licensed is invalid as derived and requires re-specification before use in any model.

KPI Formula Interpretation
loss_ratio incurred / premium LR > 1 = underwriting loss
claim_frequency claims / exposure Claims per policy year
claim_severity incurred / claims Avg cost per claim event
pure_premium incurred / exposure Risk cost per policy year
years_licensed year − lic_year Experience proxy ⚠️
licence_age age − years_lic Age at first licence

Slide 4 | Analyses Overview: Univariate

# Analysis Chart Type Rationale
4.1 Portfolio composition by policy type ggbarstats() + Pearson χ² Plain bar only answers how many; ggbarstats() tests whether bonus score composition differs significantly across types
4.2 Bonus score by business type ggbarstats() + Pearson χ² Tests whether new business carries materially worse risk profile than portfolio renewals
4.3 Geographic distribution Stacked 100% bar + count labels Proportions and absolute volumes both matter; pure proportions hide the Islands segment’s thin ~24,000-policy base
4.4 Distribution of vehicle age Histogram + density overlay Right-skewed integer variable; density curve smooths the empirical shape
4.5 Distribution of vehicle value Histogram + density (log₁₀) Mandatory log scale; two orders of magnitude spread compresses the modal range into invisibility on linear scale
4.6 Distribution of driver age Histogram + density + reference lines Reference lines at 25 and 65 make actuarial risk thresholds immediately visible

Guiding principle: Chart type is determined by the question, not convention. ggbarstats() replaces plain bars for categorical variables because the chi-square test is the primary analytical question. Log scale for vehicle value is a statistical necessity, not a stylistic choice.

Slide 6 | Univariate: Portfolio Composition

Interpretation: χ² (p < 0.001) confirms bonus composition is not independent of policy type. COMP_N carries 3.5% Bad-score policyholders; nearly 3× the rate of other types, textbook adverse selection. New Business carries 2× the Bad-score rate of Portfolio renewals (1.6% vs 0.8%), confirming the acquisition channel absorbs materially worse risk before renewal underwriting filters apply.

Slide 7 | Univariate: Geographic & Vehicle Distributions

Interpretation: Islands has only ~24,000 policies; too few for statistically reliable loss ratio estimates (wide CIs confirmed in Slide 14). Vehicle age is right-skewed (mode 20–25 yrs), indicating an older fleet where the non-linear severity curve applies at both extremes. Vehicle value is log-normally distributed (median €24,700)which makes log scale is mandatory; linear scale compresses the modal range into an unreadable sliver.

Slide 8 | Univariate: Driver Age Distribution

Portfolio is concentrated in the 35–60 band; the actuarially safest segment.

  • Under-25 drivers are markedly under-represented; higher premiums deter uptake, meaning the insurer attracts only the least price-sensitive young drivers
  • Over-65 drivers taper naturally with licence cessation

Statistical implication: The U-shaped age–risk relationship (young and old drivers claiming more) is well established. However, because both risk extremes are thinly populated here, the age signal is statistically diluted; explaining why the Spearman ρ between driver age and claim frequency is near-zero (−0.035) in Slide 12. This is a portfolio composition effect, not evidence that age is irrelevant to risk.

Slide 9 | Univariate: Summary of Findings

Variable Pattern Implication
Policy type COMP_N: 3.5% Bad; TP: 1.6% Adverse selection in comp. cover
Business type NB: 1.6% Bad vs 0.8% Portfolio Acquisition absorbs worse risk
Municipality Islands: n ≈ 24,000 only Estimates unreliable; need uncertainty buffer
Vehicle age Mode 20–25 yrs; right-skewed Non-linear severity at both extremes
Vehicle value Log-normal; median €24,700 Log-scale severity loadings required
Driver age 35–60 dominated; thin extremes U-shape diluted; signal at extremes

Cross-variable insight: An older vehicle fleet + middle-aged driver base means demographic extremes are bypassed. Risk concentration is instead occurring in the product and acquisition channel dimensions (COMP_N adverse selection, NB vs Portfolio gap).

Slide 10 | Bivariate: Loss Ratio- Policy Type & Bonus Score

Interpretation: COMP_N has the highest median loss ratio and widest violin- simultaneously the least profitable and most volatile product. Violin width reveals substantial mass above break-even, not just outliers (Kruskal-Wallis p < 0.05). Loss ratio increases monotonically Good→Bad with all pairwise tests significant. Bad-score half-eye shows a heavier right tail- bad policyholders drive disproportionate large-loss exposure, which is what drives capital requirements, not the mean.

Slide 11 | Bivariate: Claim Severity - Fuel Type & Vehicle Age

Interpretation: Diesel vehicles show statistically higher severity (Wilcoxon p = 0.04) - a consistent median location shift, not a tail effect, supporting a 5–10% diesel severity loading. Vehicle age shows a non-linear U-shape: severity peaks for new vehicles (high replacement value), declines through mid-years, then rises again for very old vehicles (rare parts, specialist labour). A simple declining age factor in the rating engine is therefore incorrect.

Slide 12 | Bivariate: Demographic Drivers

Interpretation: Ridgelines confirm the actuarial U-shape - 18–25 band widest and most right-skewed; 36–55 most compact and closest to break-even; 65+ moderately elevated. Heatmap reveals an interaction: 65+ drivers in 0–3-year vehicles show elevated claim frequency; consistent with older drivers adapting to unfamiliar new vehicle technology. Driver age and years_licensed both show near-zero Spearman ρ, a consequence of the under-25 and over-65 extremes being thinly represented in this portfolio (confirmed in Slide 8).

Slide 13 | Bivariate: Brand, Status & Behavioural Drivers

Interpretation: Brand tier does not discriminate claim frequency (all tiers identical), but Luxury’s 99% CI extends further upward for severity, confirming disproportionately costly extreme claims. Apply brand tier as a severity tail loading, not a frequency loading. Glass claimers show a bimodal distribution peaking at 1.0 and 2.0 events/year, they almost never appear at zero frequency. Glass claims are confirmed gateway events that co-occur with broader claims activity; a 10–15% frequency loading at renewal for prior-year glass claimers is supported.

Slide 14 | Bivariate: Loyalty & Geographic Drivers

Interpretation: Bad-score policyholders cancel at 25% but 75% stay; the stickiest cohort, likely lacking competitive alternatives. The insurer’s attrition process fails to shed its worst risks; actively pricing Bad-score COMP_N to not-renew is more effective than passive stickiness. Urban segments show consistently higher loss ratios than rural. Island segments have dramatically wide CIs; the observed median loss ratio is statistically unreliable; pricing should apply an explicit uncertainty buffer at the 95th percentile of the CI, not the point estimate.

Slide 15 | Conclusion & Reflection

What this exercise demonstrates

Visual analytics combined with statistical rigour, provides structured, evidence-based insights. Distributional visualisation, non-parametric testing, and explicit uncertainty quantification reveal patterns that summary statistics alone miss.

The role of the data analyst

A data analyst surfaces patterns and quantifies associations; they do not make business decisions. Translating findings into business strategies requires actuarial judgement, regulatory context, and commercial considerations beyond analytical scope.

Crucially: correlation ≠ causation e.g., glass claimers showing higher claim frequencies describes a pattern but it does not establish that glass claims cause subsequent claims. Establishing causality requires controlled study designs that cross-sectional analysis cannot provide.

Limitations

  • years_licensed mis-specified; re-derivation needed

  • Cross-sectional data; no causal inference

Further work required

🔬 Investigate interaction terms (COMP_N × Bad bonus; Luxury × Neutral) via multivariate GLM

🔬 Temporal loss ratio trend analysis across 2022–2024 to detect deteriorating segments

🔬 Apply credibility weighting to thin-data cells before pricing decisions

📊 Enrich with geospatial data to model risk at postcode level
